keep: She built her case out of what the other side had already printed about itself.
lede: She did not count the dead herself. She took the count her opponents' own press had made, and showed what it said.
copy: In 1892 three men who ran the People's Grocery outside Memphis, its president, its manager and its clerk, were taken from jail and lynched. A white grocer named Barrett kept a shop on the opposite corner and had threatened to clean them out. The wire services called the dead men toughs and desperadoes. Wells owned a share of the Memphis Free Speech, and on 21 May her paper printed an editorial on the lynchings that the white press read as an insult to white women. She was in New York on holiday. Her business manager had to leave town to escape a mob; she was warned that bodily harm awaited her if she came back; and, in her own words, creditors took possession of the office and sold the outfit.

The defence of lynching rested on one claim: that it answered the rape of white women. Wells tested it with the other side's numbers. The Chicago Tribune had compiled a count, 728 Black Americans lynched in eight years, and in 'Southern Horrors' (October 1892) she set it against the claim: only one-third of them had even been charged with rape, to say nothing of those in that third who were innocent. 'The Red Record' (1895) was subtitled 'Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching', and said its method out loud: these were compilations made by white men, of reports sent out by white men in the South, so that out of their own mouths the murderers would be condemned. Its tables give 241 people lynched in 1892, 160 of them Black, and break each year down by the offence alleged.

She is filed under activism, and the filing loses the method. The pamphlets are arguments from data, built by someone who understood that a number is only as good as whoever will accept its source, and who therefore used the source her opponents could least deny. It is the move John Snow made with a map of a pump and Nightingale made with the army's own returns, in the same half-century and against the same instinct to explain a death rate by the character of the dead. Wells made it while the people she was counting were still being killed, and with a mob's threat already on record against her.

bio.why: The long scholarly life, built on the archive rather than on the autobiography. 'Crusade for Justice', which she left unfinished and her daughter edited for publication in 1970, is her own account and worth reading beside it.

contested: How far a count made from the newspapers can be trusted, including by her. Her figures are the Chicago Tribune's, which recorded what its correspondents reported and in the terms they reported it, and missed killings nobody wrote up. The Equal Justice Initiative's modern count documented 4,075 racial terror lynchings of African Americans in twelve Southern states between 1877 and 1950, at least 800 more than the most comprehensive earlier study had found. The total her opponents supplied was too low. Whether her one-third is too high, too low or about right cannot be settled from the Tribune's lists, because the alleged offence was whatever the lynchers and the local paper said it was. She knew that, and said so: some of the third charged with rape were innocent of it.
